  • Every layer adds surface area — dependencies, caching, distribution. Exploitation gets easier, not harder, as the stack grows.
  • Defence must be comprehensive, meticulous, and regularly revised. A one-time security push is a snapshot of a moving target.
  • The leverage is in the architecture — zero trust, framework-level protections, automated discovery, threat modelling. Those reduce the number of decisions humans have to get right.
  • Specific mitigations will change as attacks shift and browsers ship built-in protections. The design philosophies — worst-case design, least authority, allowlists, verify every privileged action, test for regressions — are career-long.

Attack → defence, in one table

Every row from Part II, with the chapter of Part III that answers it. Use this as the index, not as a substitute for the detail above.

Attack (Part II)Prevent (Part III)Contain / detect
Stored / reflected XSS (ch. 10)innerText not innerHTML; sanitise with a maintained library; CSP script-srcCSP nonce/hash + report-uri; Trusted Types; safe sinks audited
DOM XSS / mXSS (ch. 10)Never pass user data to eval, DOMParser, document.write, Blob, SVG; build nodes explicitlyClient-side lint rules; CSP (partial only); code review of sinks
CSRF (ch. 11)No state change on GET; per-session CSRF token in middlewareSameSite=Strict; Origin/Referer checks; Sec-Fetch-*
XXE (ch. 12)Disable DTDs/external entities in every parserPrefer JSON; egress filtering; parser config tests
SQL injection (ch. 13)Prepared statements with bind variablesDB encoders where parameterising is impossible; least-privilege DB user
Code / command injection (ch. 13)No user command reaching a CLI; allowlist verbs, order, frequencyOne OS user per module; no shell interpolation; dependency audit
ReDoS (ch. 14)No user-supplied regex; linter for backtracking patternsRequest timeouts; input length caps
Logical DoS (ch. 14)Rank features by resource cost; cap the work a single account can triggerPer-request timing logs; quotas; async job monitoring
DDoS (ch. 14)Nothing prevents itScrubbing service; blackholing; tuned filters after measuring real traffic
Mass assignment (ch. 15)Field allowlist or DTODiff-audit what the DB layer can write; alert on privilege fields
IDOR (ch. 15)Masked references + object-level authorisationHigh-entropy ids plus rate limits; access logging
Serialization (ch. 15)Well-tested serializer, popular format, sanitise before serialisingAllowlist input types; never eval the output
Prototype pollution (ch. 16)Key allowlist; Object.create(null)Object.freeze selectively; patched merge libraries
Clickjacking (ch. 16)frame-ancestors 'none'Framebuster (legacy); Sec-Fetch-Dest checks
Tabnabbing (ch. 16)rel="noopener noreferrer" on user linksCOOP same-origin; fetch metadata isolation policies
Dependency attacks (ch. 17)Model the tree; lock + shrinkwrap; CVE scan per buildIsolate risky packages on their own server; Git SHAs or a private mirror
Business logic (ch. 18)Worst-case design in architecture; threat model per featureStatistical modelling with headless browsers; anomaly detection
Info disclosure / enumeration (ch. 23)Allowlisted generic messages; no sequential idsRate limits sized to legitimate use

The maturity ladder (author’s synthesis, not the book’s)

Part III is roughly ordered by maturity. Most teams sit on rung 2 or 3 and believe they are on 5. This framing is my summary of how the chapters build on each other.

RungWhat it looks likeWhat is still missingChapters
0 · ReactiveYou learn about bugs from customers or TwitterEverything—
1 · ConfiguredHTTPS, CSP, cookie flags, security headers, patched dependenciesNo design or review process; still finding bugs late22, 30, 33
2 · ReviewedArchitecture review + security code review at merge, with an anti-pattern checklistNothing catches logic flaws; regressions return21, 25
3 · ModeledThreat models with actors, vectors, mitigations and a delta; worst-case designDiscovery is ad hoc; no scoring, no closed loop24, 36
4 · DiscoveredStatic + dynamic analysis, disclosure programme, bounties, pen testsFixes are ad hoc; no regression tests; no metric26
5 · ManagedReproduce → CVSS → prioritised fix → regression test → trend metrics; owners and deadlinesOnly that it drifts if nobody maintains it27, 20
6 · Designed-inZero trust, least authority, allowlists, secure-by-default frameworks, per-module isolationThe next unknown attack21, 31, 34, 35
The cheapest two rungs

If you can only do two things this quarter: enable CSP with frame-ancestors 'none' and hardened cookies (an afternoon), and add a security regression test to every closed security bug (minutes each, compounding forever). Both are in the book, both are cheap, and both survive refactors better than a checklist does.
